entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Nuno Leites • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, 2d

MOTION BRANDING

Famel is a Portuguese brand focused on the motorbike industry since the 50s. The brand has become a national symbol and, even today, its motorbikes remain in the garage of many people.

The company declared bankruptcy in 2002 but, recently, was object of a total revitalization with the intention of rebuilding the whole brand and focus on the electric mobility. For this new electric era, Famel needed a rebranding that would communicate the new values and mission without erasing the rich past and legacy.

I had the privilege of being invited to take part of this creative process and think about how to elevate the brand with motion applied to the logo, social media assets, video transitions and a short motion film revealing the new brand identity.

The most important part of applying motion to the branding was to conceive small but distinctive behaviors that would emphasize freedom, speed, innovation and electric sustainable power.

entry.title: Halfbrick+ (Opener) – Dan Rice
entry.summary: Opening Sequence Decades of Halfbrick characters. One very crowded screen. The opening sequence for Halfbrick+ mixes 2D, 3D, frame by frame, puppet animation, pixel art and simulated practical effects, like paper tearing. “Goal: Make a memorable launch experience so awesome that
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Dan Rice • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, Titles, Mixed Media

Opening Sequence

Decades of Halfbrick characters. One very crowded screen. The opening sequence for Halfbrick+ mixes 2D, 3D, frame by frame, puppet animation, pixel art and simulated practical effects, like paper tearing.

“Goal: Make a memorable launch experience so awesome that people won't skip it even if they've seen it before.”

— Halfbrick Marketing Team

Halfbrick invited me to pitch on the opening sequence for their subscription platform, Halfbrick+.

Like most people, I was blown away the first time I played Fruit Ninja, so the chance to help shape how players are welcomed to the platform was a thrill.

The brief from Halfbrick’s marketing team was for an opening sequence that's exciting and celebrates everything Halfbrick. The answer was to bring nearly every character from their games together in one sequence.

There is no one art style that defines a Halfbrick game. Characters from decades of games each come from their own world, with their own look.

My pitch was a bricollage: a mixed media sequence that brings every character into the same space without losing what makes each one distinctive. We took the worlds and interfaces players already know and remixed them.

It also let us mix animation styles freely, from cel and puppet animation to UI animation and 3D.

“BRICOLAGE (bree-koh-LAHZH)”

— NOUN: CONSTRUCTION (AS OF A SCULPTURE OR A STRUCTURE OF IDEAS) ACHIEVED BY USING WHATEVER COMES TO HAND.

THE PITCH

Initial Design

Nobody knows the Halfbrick brand better than the people behind it, so I brought them into the process.

Drawing on my work with startups, I ran workshops with the team. We began with a kickoff to pin down what they wanted the sequence to achieve and hear their first ideas. Then we ran a brainstorm to dig up scenes, scenarios, funny moments and Easter eggs that felt true to the characters and games.

One of my favourites which made the final cut: Sensei riding on top of Colossotron like Paul Atreides on a sandworm.

I developed the visual story structure with Halfbrick’s Brendan Deboy. Starting from the rough boards and animatic from my pitch, plus the updated narrative from the workshops, Brendan sketched the first pass of the boards. From there we went back and forth, refining the sequence until the story structure was locked.

PRE-PRODUCTION

Boardimatic

PRE-PRODUCTION

Styleframes

PRODUCTION

Character Animation

I wanted the opener to feel like a Saturday-morning cartoon intro crossed with a roller-coaster ride: fast, loud and impossible to skip.

I directed the piece, and I also cut it, composited it and handled the 3D. Each artist’s shots went straight into the timeline as they landed, so I could judge them in context, tighten the timing frame by frame and send back precise notes. With one person carrying every shot through to the final composite, the sequence holds together from first frame to last.

Transitions turn a string of scenes into a ride. Every cut hands its energy to the next shot, using match cuts, colour matches, movement matches and cuts on action.

Barry rips his shirt, and the tear splits the screen like paper to reveal Colossotron. Sensei lifts an apple, we crash zoom into it, and the red colour matches to a button. A bear flies at the camera, we enter its mouth, and a fish swimming past match cuts to a bomb.

The edit only stops once. Dan the Man’s fly kick cracks the screen to white, then the rapid-fire ending kicks in.

Halfbrick+ is built for mobile, so the opener had to hold up on everything from small phones to tablets. I kept the most important element of every shot in the centre of frame. It gives the sequence its ride-like momentum, and it means nothing gets cropped on any screen.

We delivered five versions, set up so the Halfbrick team can create any other format they need without coming back to me.

entry.title: Wide Awake: Night Shift – Make Good Studio
entry.summary: MAKE GOOD / ORIGINAL CONCEPT FILM A man wakes up on an alien operating table. The crew has a more pressing problem: coffee. The wrong emergency We started with a man waking up somewhere he absolutely should not be. To him, it is the worst moment of his life. To the aliens standin
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Make Good Studio • Categoría: Commercial

MAKE GOOD / ORIGINAL CONCEPT FILM

A man wakes up on an alien operating table. The crew has a more pressing problem: coffee.

The wrong emergency

We started with a man waking up somewhere he absolutely should not be. To him, it is the worst moment of his life. To the aliens standing over him, it is another night at work. Their argument is about decaf, loyalty points and a birthday muffin. The more ordinary the conversation becomes, the stranger his situation feels. That became the idea behind Wide Awake, a fictional coffee brand for the night shift.

Three different priorities

One alien wants coffee that will keep them awake. The other wants the rewards. The patient just wants to go home. Giving each character something different to care about kept the scene simple. We developed character sheets and room references before building the shots. The faces, uniforms, pajamas and operating table had to belong to the same world, even as the camera moved from the patient’s point of view to the aliens’ conversation.

Finding the conversation

The aliens needed to sound like coworkers, not villains. We used ElevenLabs Flows to audition voices for each character, then generated the full conversation with multiple speakers. Hearing the replies together gave us a way to judge the exchanges as a scene. The direction became quite specific. One voice was too theatrical, so we pulled it toward an everyday delivery. “And a birthday muffin” needed to sound like a reasonable justification. We adjusted the synthesis spelling of “decaf” to fix a consonant and tried several versions of the pause in “But… we work nights.” Those recordings also became acting references for the animated dialogue shots. The video models generated dialogue of their own, so the finished soundtrack is not simply the original ElevenLabs conversation laid over pictures. We selected and trimmed the takes in the edit. The patient’s plea took more work. We revised the starting image to keep his face and proportions natural, then used his character sheet, the room reference and a recorded dialogue guide for the new take. His shoulders lift, his hands press into the mattress and he asks to go home. We wanted urgency without a cartoon grimace.

A room that holds together

The camera begins where the patient is, looking up into surgical lights. Other angles let us watch the coffee dispute while keeping him in the scene. The table, lamps and curved doorway give the room recognizable landmarks. We used room references alongside the character sheets to guide the generated shots. The goal was a sequence that feels like one scene, with the same people, clothes and surroundings from angle to angle. Small changes in eyelines or body proportions can break that feeling, even when an individual image looks convincing.

Making the coffee feel real

Wide Awake needed an identity that could carry the final shot. A coffee bean with a lightning bolt gives the brand a simple mark. Brown lettering, a cream bag and a sage mug bring some warmth into the metal room. The decaf pouch is the problem driving the conversation. The closing product shot gives us the answer: Night Shift coffee. We kept the camera movement gentle and let the steam and packaging bring the film to a quieter finish.

Letting the joke land

The edit moves between panic and small talk. A reaction can be funnier than another line, and the pause after a ridiculous answer matters as much as the answer itself. The patient’s interruption brings us back to what everyone else in the room has forgotten. Generated dialogue takes needed editorial attention too. Repeated words and unwanted speech at the ends of takes were trimmed so each exchange stayed clean. Dialogue, the room ambience, effects and music were balanced in the final edit, keeping the conversation easy to follow before the product finish. The sound also had to put the voices inside the ship. Josh added a little reverb by hand so they felt part of the metal interior. Spaceship ambience and a very subtle rustle from the coffee bag gave the scene texture without competing with the conversation.

entry.summary: I was commissioned to create this explainer video for Mediterranean Algae, a cleantech company working to improve ocean health through technology. The challenge was to turn complex marine biotechnology into a clear and engaging story, connecting environmental monitoring, ocean re
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Lutosfera • Categoría: Commercial • Especialidad: Brand Film, Product Videos, BTS

I was commissioned to create this explainer video for Mediterranean Algae, a cleantech company working to improve ocean health through technology.

The challenge was to turn complex marine biotechnology into a clear and engaging story, connecting environmental monitoring, ocean regeneration, and circular economy through motion design.

How do you make complex marine biotechnology easy to understand?

Mediterranean Algae brings together environmental monitoring, marine bioremediation, and biomass valorization. The challenge was to connect these technologies into one clear story while communicating their value to an industrial and institutional audience.

From idea to frame.

Every animation starts with an idea. The storyboards helped shape the narrative, explore compositions, and define how each scene would connect with the next.

This stage was all about finding the right visual flow before bringing everything to life.

Inside After Effects, individual elements, camera movements, and transitions come together to build the final piece.

From organizing compositions to fine-tuning the smallest details, this is where the different scenes start to feel like one cohesive story.

Motion becomes the tool that connects every part of the story.

Camera movements reveal the wider coastal environment, transitions guide the viewer between technologies, and animated data elements make complex processes easier to follow.

Each sequence builds on the previous one, turning three distinct solutions into one connected vision for ocean health.

entry.title: NUVO: Find your space – Make Good Studio
entry.summary: MAKE GOOD / ORIGINAL CONCEPT FILM A room comes apart. A world opens up. An original headphone concept from Make Good. The idea There’s a moment when you put on headphones and everything around you feels a little further away. We wanted to take that feeling literally. NUVO begins
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Make Good Studio • Categoría: Commercial

MAKE GOOD / ORIGINAL CONCEPT FILM

A room comes apart. A world opens up. An original headphone concept from Make Good.

The idea

There’s a moment when you put on headphones and everything around you feels a little further away. We wanted to take that feeling literally. NUVO begins in a cramped room, with a phone interrupting an already crowded desk. She puts on her headphones, the walls pull away, and suddenly there’s room to breathe.

Finding the look

We started with purple headphones, warm metal details and a city lit in blue and pink. The crescent on the earcup found its way into the NUVO wordmark. From there, we worked out the character and her surroundings. Looking at the boards together helped us catch the little things that changed between shots: how the headphones sat, where the chair was, which way she was facing.

Opening up the room

The room coming apart was the shot we spent the most time on. We wanted the walls to move away while she stayed right where she was. We built a simple 3D version to work out the camera move and the order things would leave. That gave us a guide for the AI footage. It took several passes to find a take where the movement felt right.

Giving it time

The opening moves quickly: the room, the phone, the headphones. Then we slow down and let the walls fall away. That’s the moment the film has been building toward, so we gave it time. The music opens up with the room. Small sounds like the phone, her hands and a breath keep it personal, even as the world gets much bigger.

“Give it something worth hearing.”

— NUVO: FIND YOUR SPACE

entry.title: The long, icy life of a fusilli – thijs merckx
entry.summary: SMILING COOK A two-minute explainer that follows one fusilli from wheat field to plate and makes chefs rethink the word "frozen". The Brief Smiling Cook makes pasta and sauces for professional kitchens. Their fresh pasta is cooked al dente and then frozen quickly. This gives them
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: thijs merckx • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: 2d

SMILING COOK

A two-minute explainer that follows one fusilli from wheat field to plate and makes chefs rethink the word "frozen".

The Brief

Smiling Cook makes pasta and sauces for professional kitchens. Their fresh pasta is cooked al dente and then frozen quickly. This gives them two strong claims: the pasta stays fresh for 18 months, and it's ready to serve in 30 seconds. Genius! But there's a problem. To a chef, "frozen" sounds like a compromise. The film had to turn it into the reason to buy.

During the intake I got to know the product and its perks. We discussed how it's produced, distributed and prepared, and I got a real feel for the people who buy and use the pasta.

That day I learned that chefs are busy people and, apparently, want only three things from a video: get to the point fast, don't overcomplicate things, and make them smile.
Oh, and they hate being sold to.

““Freezing isn't a compromise. It's the reason to buy.””

Chefs want the point first, so the film opens with the promise: 18 months fresh, 30 seconds to serve. Then it rewinds to the source of all good pasta: golden wheat, ground into flour.

I kept sentences short, hopping from one production step to the next, and broke them up with casual remarks from the narrator like "Okay, not NO time". This gave the writing a natural flow, as if you were being spoken to by the Smiling Cook himself.

I wrote the voice-over in English and Dutch side by side, so the wordplay and timing work in both languages.

“"It’s fresh frozen. Yes, exactly, fresh and frozen."”

I wanted to stick close to the subject of the film: a single fusilli. So I kept the camera on that one piece of pasta while the world around it transformed, creating one continuous motion with hardly any cuts.

Time is the film's second character. It flows gently during production but stops whenever the pasta freezes. At those moments I slowed the world around the fusilli right down, so you feel time standing still. The kitchen time-lapse is the exception. There I sped the world up instead: life rushes by while the pasta waits patiently in the freezer.

Visually, I wanted a simple look that guides the eye. A warm golden yellow makes the product the star, while shades of grey and crisp line work keep the world around it clean. A cold blue marks the freezing moments, and green adds some flavour when the sauces and ingredients arrive.

To make sure the timing and copy would work, I drew an animatic in Procreate Dreams and cut it to a scratch voice-over. By the time animation started, I had resolved most of the mismatches between animation and voice-over.

As always, animation brought surprises and hurdles. The shot in the factory turned out to be too long for the voice-over, so I had to rework the layout. Other tweaks were needed, but all changes served the brief.

The film was delivered in English, Dutch, French and German, each in landscape, square and portrait, ready for the website and every social feed. I planned the layouts for all three crops from the start, so nothing important falls off the edge on a phone.

entry.summary: At MediaNerd, we spend most of our time showing off what we can do for our clients, so we thought it was about time we did the same for ourselves. We gave ourselves a simple brief: make bumper-to-bumper traffic worth watching. Then we ripped away restrictions and let the ideas fl
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Adam Kelly • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, 3d, 2d

At MediaNerd, we spend most of our time showing off what we can do for our clients, so we thought it was about time we did the same for ourselves. We gave ourselves a simple brief: make bumper-to-bumper traffic worth watching. Then we ripped away restrictions and let the ideas flow freely. The result? A tux-wearing octopus butler, a flying taxi, and a full showcase of 2D and 3D animation skills.

It always starts with the story and we kept this one simple by contrasting the tedium experienced in traffic jams, with the magical, exciting worlds animation can build.

We’ll be honest, not every creative process includes discussion around how an octopus would fit into a tuxedo, but once we’d established what tentacles went where, the team went about flexing their 2D and 3D animation skills.

Playing to everyone’s strengths and showcasing a range of skills, we brought the story to life by utilising traditional software craft and a little bit of emerging tech for the final look of the car smoke.

Nobody wants to be animating several cars by hand, so we constructed a system based around a handful of splines.

The roads, barriers and streetlights we all tied to a central spline. Then instances of the vehicles were placed within a system of cloners and offset accordingly.

We fed user colour data into a ramp to control the colour of the vehicles, which made the whole scene a lot easier to deal with.

entry.title: The Climate-Health Nexus | Chapter Zero + Wellcome Trust – Viral Mistry
entry.summary: Recent heatwaves have shown climate change as a rising risk to human health. Chapter Zero and Wellcome wanted to bring that truth to the private sector with an impactful film. The Wellcome Trust funds science on how climate change affects health. Chapter Zero brings climate aware
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Viral Mistry • Categoría: Film • Especialidad: Documentary

Recent heatwaves have shown climate change as a rising risk to human health. Chapter Zero and Wellcome wanted to bring that truth to the private sector with an impactful film.

The Wellcome Trust funds science on how climate change affects health. Chapter Zero brings climate awareness into the boardroom. Together they formed a partnership to highlight the human aspects of climate-health governance and business.

I edited this short film as the centrepiece of a flagship event in front of 300 board members, including more than 50 FTSE 350 Chairs and non-executives, and later in the Wellcome Trust boardroom, where it received a standing ovation.

The post-shoot workflow begins with a transcript of all interviews which averaged at around 15 minutes per person

and I ask the client to highlight which lines they think most important to use with an eye on a film no longer than 3-4 minutes' duration. Compiling those client selects, the first edit ran to 11 minutes so I set to work distilling all that down to its core essence, removing repetition where more than one person made the same point, removing extraneous detail, tightening up those micro pauses, resulting in a 5 minute-long edit then eventually 3.5 minutes.

Narrative structure

Bypassing a typical documentary approach, I wanted the audience to feel uncomfortable, tense, from the first few seconds onwards, to throw you into a narrative with urgent pacing; the result is a film that feels more like a trailer.

The audience needs context, and Director of Climate and Health at Wellcome, Alan Dangour was an obvious choice to begin the film with - bold, assertive, instantly compelling - setting out the tone of everything that follows. Engineer and angel investor Magali Anderson told a particularly emotive story of real loss, and I had it saved for the film’s conclusion. It was actually the client who suggested we place this up front, and I saw that it worked much better. Trailer edits often work like this; 180º swings that trigger dopamine hits and retain audience attention.

Filmed but not used was the Netflix-style sit-down shots – an overused cliché that certainly has its place, but in this urgent narrative I thought it too contrived.
I did however use 'in-between' moments during the film of participants - pausing, thinking, looking - to evoke a sense of uneasiness.

Soundscapes

Whilst happy with a music track I sourced for the main body of the film, we felt it needed a greater sense of tension.

To achieve this I added a ticking clock mechanism along with a drone noise using the 'Shepard tone' effect, which is the auditory illusion of a tone that seems to ascend in pitch endlessly and with increasing intensity. Understated so as to not compete with the music or dialogue, it's much more felt than heard, adding urgency to the dialogue.

For this particular section, I added carefully-timed audio moments to underscore the story, without going overboard to draw attention away from the dialogue.

Each of the 300 board members in that room helps decide how a company treats its people, its supply chain and its customers.

Many sit on more than one board. One film, seen by the right people, can travel into hundreds of boardrooms and instigate systemic change.

entry.summary: Client: Edward Jones, USA Creative Agency: Bulldog Media, UK Illustrator & Animator: Dan See This is the second animation in a series of three explainer animations for Edward Jones. The idea was to develop a less playful, more premium style reflective of the slightly more retro t
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Dan See • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: 2d, Motion Design, 3d

Client: Edward Jones, USA Creative Agency: Bulldog Media, UK Illustrator & Animator: Dan See

This is the second animation in a series of three explainer animations for Edward Jones. The idea was to develop a less playful, more premium style reflective of the slightly more retro theme of the 1960s. Drawing inspiration from Saul Bass's title sequences and Pan Am Airways graphic posters, we developed a style in line with the Edward Jones brand. Utilising AI in the design stage proved to be highly beneficial in developing this reference style, which was rather unique to this client and different from past content created for them. Working closely with Bulldog Agency and two other animators, who were responsible for explainer 1 and 3, we managed to knuckle down the style and develop three synergetic animations. (Unfortunately video 1 and 3 are not available for preview in this study).

Working with screens from past Edward Jones animations and blending them with the retro 60s style, an overall Edward Jones mood storyboard was generated to encapsulate the general idea and build a baseline from which to begin.

Strategic Advice was originally going to be more blue-focused, whereas the first one in the series was more yellow-focused (all according to Edward Jones brand guidelines). At the end of the project, it was decided that all three animations would use the yellow hues as the primary colours, and the blue hues would remain as secondary colours. As you can see, this adjustment was made directly to the animation before final delivery.

The full animation was created in Adobe After Effects, using 2D and 3D
animation and a lot of precomps :) The majority of all three animations were created without AI assistance, but AI generative tools were used to add motion to the various figures, such as the mountain climbers.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Dan See • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: 2d, 3d, Motion Design

Client: Edward Jones, USA Creative Agency: Bulldog Media, UK Illustration & Animation: Dan See

Edward Jones wanted to create an animation explaining their Investment Advisory Program (IPA) which combines all their programs into one main program in which services could be tailored to meet each client's personal needs. After recently completing a series of animations describing these various singular programs, they wanted to keep s similar style, but explore the world of gamification as a metaphor for the different "levels" or programs being brought together into a single "game". After utilising an isometric design style in past animations for the same client, we decided to go down the route of designing a 8-bit gaming world, using isometric blocks and designs to bring together a variety of well-known old-school style games to symbolise the different Edward Jones' solutions.

Often an idea, once formulated on paper or on screen, doesn't materialise in the way that was initially visualised. The excitement of that idea or style ends up not working as a concept for a particular client, brand or subject matter, and we are reverted back to the drawing board to build something more visually appropriate. The gaming-style animation evolved to be more aligned to the client's corporate and financial identity, with a subtle hint of this 8-bit gaming metaphor. This new design ended up being a wonderful addition to the other creative content we had developed for them in the past, blending a variety of approaches that were used previously.

The full animation was created in Adobe After Effects, using 2D and 3D
animation and a range of plugins (Newton, as an example). AI was also used minimally to create small animated assets to insert into scenes here and there.

And that's it! Thanks for viewing :)

entry.content:

A set of five ads for VOD plus social media cutdowns.

Coffee and TV brought me in to assemble and direct a team of animators to bring EON Next's playful characters to life for this set of TV ads. It was a joy to cram lots of info into these punchy spots, while keeping it fun and engaging.

The client was keen to zoom into the cable in the Solar Max video to take us from external shot to internal, but we felt a 3D look would be too far off-brand from EON's clean, vector look. We decided to find a solution entirely inside After Effects.

I rigged a series of solids with circular mattes stacked above one another, and used a nifty little expression to tell the mattes to follow a control layer with a slight delay. This meant I could animate the control layer's position to determine the winding direction of the tunnel as we shoot through it.

entry.title: Cinanima '26 – Studio Kimchi
entry.summary: The official promotional film for the festival's 50th edition. (Not just) another festival intro. For its 50th edition, Cinanima asked us to make the festival's official promotional film, which screens before every session. We've attended the festival for years, so we built the f
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Studio Kimchi • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: 2d, 3d, Stop Motion

The official promotional film for the festival's 50th edition.

(Not just) another festival intro.

For its 50th edition, Cinanima asked us to make the festival's official promotional film, which screens before every session. We've attended the festival for years, so we built the film around what that experience actually feels like: the trip to Espinho, finding your seat, and watching animated films on the big screen with a room full of animation fans. The characters mirror the audience experience.

Story first.

Story first We broke the CINANIMA logo down into geometric pieces and turned each one into a character, knowing they would reunite at the end to form the logo. Because the concept was so visual, we went straight to storyboards. A rough first pass blocked out the sequence, and from there we boarded the full film.

Setting the scene.

Cinanima has been held for many years at the Centro Multimeios in Espinho, in northern Portugal. We researched the real locations and designed and painted every background from them, translated into a cartoon style.

Mixed 2D/3D animation approach.

The film combines several techniques and was made with many of our regular collaborators. Wide shots use a hybrid approach: character bodies were animated and rendered in 3D, while legs and faces were animated in 2D. Close-ups and medium shots are traditional 2D animation, taken from rough animation through clean-up to color. With so many artists involved, we let each one work in their preferred tools, which meant Maya and Blender for 3D, and Photoshop, Blender, TVPaint, Toon Boom and Procreate Dreams for 2D. All compositing was done in Blackmagic Fusion.

The shortest short film block.

In the film, our characters sit down to watch a short film program, the kind of block that mixes authors, styles and techniques. To represent one, we made one. We invited ten animators to each create a one-second film in their own style. Each received the same abstract base animation to interpret however they wanted, without seeing or knowing anything about the other nine pieces.

The TV spot.

To advertise the event on TV, radio and online, we also created a shorter 20s version. This version includes all the excitement of the characters traveling to the festival and getting ready to watch the films, but leaves the audience wanting more, not revealing the films behind the curtain.

entry.title: And Beyond – Sean Van Praag
entry.summary: BLINK 2024 I was commissioned to create this projection mapping piece for Blink 2024 in Cincinnati, continuing the absurd, weird energy of my previous piece, To The Moon. The whole thing was built from scratch for the building, with a loose, experimental approach that let the arc
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Sean Van Praag • Categoría: Experiences • Especialidad: Event

BLINK 2024

I was commissioned to create this projection mapping piece for Blink 2024 in Cincinnati, continuing the absurd, weird energy of my previous piece, To The Moon. The whole thing was built from scratch for the building, with a loose, experimental approach that let the architecture dictate what stayed, what changed, and what got weird.

The Concept

For this piece, I kept the process loose. I start with a pile of ideas and let the building decide which ones live. Out of every ten, maybe one or two survive the architecture. For this reason, and my own artistic preference for what I enjoy making, I tend to intentionally avoid locking into a specific theme or a story. The style tends to follow this same throughline, creating a cohesively incohesive, fresh, digital mixed-media approach. It's a lot of experimenting, seeing what works, and more often than not, what doesn't. Then figuring out how to mash it all together.

The Environment

The Blink environment can be a bit crazy. There's a lot going on and a lot of people. There are street lights, car lights, giant projectors on giant scaffolding, and storefronts glowing everywhere, with people constantly moving, drinking, and chatting. The piece plays on a loop, so there's no official start. Some people walk up a minute in, some three minutes in, and a few lucky ones catch it right at the beginning. And with 90+ installations across the festival, there's a lot competing for their time. I tried to keep it high-energy and fast-paced, no matter when someone walks up, something exciting is happening. Short and sweet.

The Building

I try to avoid simply cropping graphics into certain portions of the building. Whenever possible, I want the actual animation to move and bend with the architecture of the building. Things break and hit windows as they fall. Objects and graphics are dynamically boxed into sections of the building and bounce off walls. Windows are the trickiest part of a building like this. Some have lights on, some have curtains, some show nothing, so I assume little will show up on them. As a general rule of thumb, I've found three things hold up consistently well: • Large scale graphics that cover huge sections of the building • Graphics designed specifically for the space between the windows • Abstract designs, particles, or patterns where we don't need to see all of it What tends to fail are medium sized graphics. Half of one can disappear behind a window and you can't tell what you're looking at. Every element was built from scratch for this building.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: The Heist • Categoría: Film • Especialidad: Shorts, Experimental, BTS

HALF REZ 2026

HalfRez is one of those rare industry events where networking rarely feels like networking. Creatives come together to meet new collaborators, reconnect with familiar faces, learn something new and leave inspired. That sense of community shaped our presentation. Rather than explain every frame, we used the film to open an honest conversation about creative confidence, uncertainty, career longevity and changing tools, leaving space for attendees to see their own experiences in the story. It was a reminder that ours is a small, strange, deeply specific industry, and there is real value in finding your people within it.

A Room Full of People Who Get It

HalfRez is one of those rare industry events where networking rarely feels like networking. Creatives come together to meet new collaborators, reconnect with familiar faces, learn something new and leave inspired. That sense of community shaped our presentation. Rather than explain every frame, we used the film to open an honest conversation about creative confidence, uncertainty, career longevity and changing tools, leaving space for attendees to see their own experiences in the story. It was a reminder that ours is a small, strange, deeply specific industry, and there is real value in finding your people within it.

The project started with a stack of ideas and a room full of people willing to build on one another’s instincts. From there, the work moved through Cinema 4D, Houdini, Procreate, After Effects, Blender, and Rive, with each tool helping solve a different part of the story. The real fun was in figuring out how those worlds could connect, and how we could connect more easily while making them. We shared techniques, learned new ones, and found that a few of the best ideas appeared somewhere between “Can you show me how you did that?” and “Wait, what if we tried this?” The film is a record of that collaboration, but so is the team we became while making it.

“"The goal was not uniformity. It was unity"”

We didn’t stop at the film. Using Rive, our motion and development teams built a custom interactive experience accessed through a QR code. Attendees could visit our website or take a quick quiz to discover their “season,” then download the corresponding artwork as a wallpaper. It gave us a chance to experiment with a new tool, bring our teams closer together and give the HalfRez crowd something extra to take home.

“The weather will change. The sunlight will return. And somewhere beneath the surface, even when we cannot see it yet, something is still growing.”

entry.title: Casio - Form | Function | Fun – Lamek Felix
entry.summary: CREATIVE CAMPAIGN EXPLORATION An independent campaign study on how an icon can evolve without losing what makes it recognizable. THE IDEA An icon is never finished. The CASIO A168 is immediately recognizable. Its proportions, digital display and straightforward functionality have
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Lamek Felix • Categoría: Commercial • Especialidad: Ad, Product Videos, Brand Film

CREATIVE CAMPAIGN EXPLORATION

An independent campaign study on how an icon can evolve without losing what makes it recognizable.

THE IDEA

An icon is never finished.

The CASIO A168 is immediately recognizable.

Its proportions, digital display and straightforward functionality have given it a visual identity that does not need to be reinvented.

That became the starting point for this project.

Instead of redesigning the watch, I wanted to explore how a different visual world could change the way we perceive its character.

Color, geometry, transparency, repetition and movement became the tools for that transformation.

The product remains familiar.

The perception around it changes.

VISUAL PREMISE

FORM | FUNCTION | FUN

Form gave it structure. Function gave it purpose. Fun gave it character.

Bauhaus is often remembered through simplicity, geometry and function. But its visual language was also filled with color, movement and experimentation. That contrast felt particularly relevant to the A168. The watch is already direct, functional and instantly recognizable. The opportunity was not to make it more sophisticated, but to reveal a more playful, graphic and expressive side of the character already present in the product.

COLOR & CHARACTER

The identity remains. The character changes.

Color became one of the simplest ways to change the emotional reading of the same object.

The form remains familiar, but each variation shifts the personality of the A168.

More energetic. More graphic. More playful.

The product stays recognizable while its character moves.

A strong visual direction should survive beyond a single frame.

The goal was not to create one beautiful image. Geometry, primary colors, transparency, repetition and graphic contrast became a set of visual rules that could work across different compositions, scales and formats. The individual images change. The visual world remains consistent.

RHYTHM & REPETITION

One icon. Many expressions.

Repetition allowed the familiar silhouette of the A168 to behave almost like a graphic element.

It could multiply, overlap, change scale, change color and move through the frame without losing recognition.

The watch became both product and visual motif.

Familiar form. Different physical presence.

Transparency introduced another layer to the visual language. The silhouette remains familiar, but the way light travels through the watch changes its physical presence. Material was treated as part of the character of the campaign, not simply as decoration.

Motion allowed the same visual rules to evolve over time.

Repetition became rhythm.

Geometry became transition.

Color became progression.

The film was designed as an extension of the visual system rather than a separate expression.

“An icon is never finished.”

— LAMEK FELIX

The goal was never a single beautiful film.

From the beginning, the visual language was designed to extend beyond one format. The same direction could move across hero film, key visuals, vertical content, social assets and digital applications while keeping the same character. The project became an exercise in building a campaign system, not a collection of unrelated renders.

BEHIND THE IMAGE

From idea to execution.

Direction first. Technique in service of the idea.

The process combined creative direction, CGI, animation, look development, lighting and compositing. Each technical decision had to support the same objective: make the world around the A168 feel different without losing the product itself.

FINAL THOUGHT

An icon is never finished.

An iconic product does not always need reinvention.

Sometimes the opportunity is simply to reveal something that was already there.

The A168 remains familiar.

Its identity remains intact.

But a different visual world creates a different cultural reading.

That was the idea behind the project.

entry.title: Winter Storm Colbert – Mike Emerick
entry.summary: THE WEATHER CHANNEL + STEPHEN COLBERT A late-night joke about your brand can be a PR problem. Or it can be an invitation. “"Turns out, they've got a sense of humor."” — STEPHEN COLBERT, ON THE WEATHER CHANNEL It was also occasionally controversial. In March 2017, Winter Storm Ste
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Mike Emerick • Categoría: Commercial • Especialidad: Social, Event, Ad

THE WEATHER CHANNEL + STEPHEN COLBERT

A late-night joke about your brand can be a PR problem. Or it can be an invitation.

“"Turns out, they've got a sense of humor."”

— STEPHEN COLBERT, ON THE WEATHER CHANNEL

It was also occasionally controversial.

In March 2017, Winter Storm Stella was hitting the Northeast, putting that naming convention squarely in the national spotlight.

Stephen Colbert noticed.

Moments like that usually create a familiar choice for a brand:

Ignore the joke and let it pass, or respond by explaining why the brand was right.

The Weather Channel's president, Dave Clark, saw an opportunity immediately and asked our marketing team to explore a response. That alone changed the frame.

I hadn’t assumed a response would be on the table for The Weather Channel. Let alone something playful. Rather than default to defending the brand, Dave recognized there might be a more unexpected way in, possibly a funny one, and gave us room to find it.

This is my favorite creative space to work in: the challenge is clear, the answer isn't, and humor is an option. But this one came with a high bar.

We were responding to one of the funniest people on television.

“Pretty funny for a brand” wasn't going to cut it.

FINDING THE OPENING

Colbert had already given us the setup years earlier.

I'd followed Colbert's work since the 1990s, and I knew that mobilizing his viewers to get his name attached to things had been a recurring part of his comedy.

That gave me the opening.

If Colbert thought naming winter storms was ridiculous, maybe the best response was to show him just how ridiculous it could get:

Name one after him.

THE RESPONSE

Forecasting Winter Storm Colbert.

“"It's gonna blow hard, but have little to no impact."”

— TOM NIZIOL, ON WINTER STORM COLBERT

THE REACTION

The response became the story.

“"Brilliantly pokes fun at Stephen Colbert."”

— A.V. CLUB

““Today’s forecast across the country? Shade, shade, shade.””

— LOS ANGELES TIMES

““Came in much harder than expected.””

— VULTURE ON THE WEATHER CHANNEL

Best of all, Colbert brought the story back to The Late Show.

The idea had enough runway that we were already exploring a second act for the following season's naming cycle, this time with Colbert as a participant rather than just the subject.

THE CREATIVE LOGIC

Accept the premise and escalate it.

We used the familiar language and conventions of a Weather Channel forecast, and delivered a deadpan assessment of his professional life as if it were an actual storm.

The weather graphics, the forecast language, the storm-naming convention itself.

None of it was just decoration. It was the joke.

The response needed to feel unmistakably like The Weather Channel.

We weren't trying to imitate a late-night show.

We were using our brand language to enter his joke.

The references rewarded Colbert fans without requiring everyone else to do homework: specific enough for him, clear enough for everyone else.

Most importantly, the response needed to land while the moment was still fresh. But speed couldn’t become an excuse for something merely “good enough for social.”

So the standard wasn't, “Can we get something out quickly?”

It was, “Can we move fast and still make something Colbert might actually engage with?”

MAKING IT REAL

The idea had to move fast. So did the team.

Our marketing team, along with production, design, social and PR, helped turn it around fast enough to stay inside the moment while keeping it recognizably Weather Channel.

WHAT WE LEARNED

The real lesson wasn't speed. It was judgment.

You have to know which moments are worth entering, understand the audience well enough to enter credibly, and know your own brand well enough that the response feels authentic instead of opportunistic.

Colbert's comedy gave us the opening. The Weather Channel's forecast language gave us the structure. Dave made space to act. Tom gave the joke credibility. And the team moved fast enough to make it matter.

There was another lesson for me in it, too.

Before Dave opened the door, a response like this hadn't even occurred to me as something The Weather Channel might do. It reminded me that sometimes the boundaries around an idea are the ones you've assumed, not the ones anyone actually set.

Colbert’s monologue could have been treated as something to defend against.

Instead, we treated it as an invitation.

And sometimes the best response to a joke is understanding it well enough to make the joke bigger.

entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Mateus Klein • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Motion Design, Mixed Media, 2d

LAUGHING AND LEARNING

History with Leonardo Lima is a YouTube channel about... history, created by the teacher... you guessed it, Leonardo Lima. Léo is a great friend who not only possesses immense charisma but also has enviable teaching skills. His passion for education led him to create content for social media, aiming to democratize knowledge and explore new formats - where he can connect with his other interests such as culture, games, music, etc.

When charisma teaches

The main inspirations for the visual identity were Léo's own approach, which includes the use of anecdotes and jokes to engage the students' interest, and his equivalent among the learners, that student who expresses humor through doodles in their notebook.

Doodles in the corners of each page, faces of great figures, highlighted notes, post-its all over the place... every detail was handpicked to translate the mind of an interesting teacher (who once was an interested student).

Process Breakdown

Leaving the screen for some time, actually drawing things on paper and taking photos of my own hand? That's what I call a fun project.

The best part certainly was being able to explore a true mixed-media workflow. The original intention was to use even more analogue elements, but it was fun to simulate different physical aspects of paper stop-motion, such as:

- Low framerate (and different framerates for each element) - Distortion caused by ripples on the paper (and I have to thank Ben Mariott for this one!) - Realistic shadows - Working with multiple layers of paper and hand-drawn elements.

entry.summary: Getting the most out of a single idea “Playing with your perception and expectations, Brussels-based designer/digital artist Boris Wilmot constructs a tense, slow-building open for director Stephan Castang’s black comedy thriller Vincent Doit Mourir.” — STEPHEN PRICE - STASH MEDI
entry.content:
Estudio / Creador: Boris Wilmot • Categoría: Animation • Especialidad: Titles

Getting the most out of a single idea

“Playing with your perception and expectations, Brussels-based designer/digital artist Boris Wilmot constructs a tense, slow-building open for director Stephan Castang’s black comedy thriller Vincent Doit Mourir.”

— STEPHEN PRICE - STASH MEDIA

Vincent Borel is a graphic designer in Lyon who finds that everyone, starting with his coworkers but soon expanding out into the wider community, suddenly wants to kill him for no obvious reason

"I want an abstract opening sequence inspired by the classic
titles for Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Nortwest by Saul Bass".

That is the first thing director Stephan Castang told me.

"The sequence would introduce the urban universe Vincent is living in, his work as a graphic designer, as well as question the viewer’s gaze.
And it would end up on the screen of Vincent’s laptop."

Ok. Well I guess I should start by watching North by Nortwest again...

This is the central question throughout the whole movie.
Stephan and I wanted it to be reflected in this sequence as well.

As a fan of Saul Bass' work, being asked to re-interpret one of his title sequence is a tricky thing.

I was both super enthusiast and scared by this brief. I took the core of Bass’ opening : “lines drawing a building” and worked on this idea but with contemporary techniques.

I liked the idea of distorting reality, to the point where you cannot recognize the subject anymore. It shifts to something new. I thought it fit with the movie where this absurd starting point “everyone wants to beat me” completely transforms Vincent’s life.

So I took urban footages and started distorting them. I had in mind the slit scan videos by François Vogel (I’m a big fan!).
Stephan had already worked on the obsessive soundtrack with composer John Kaced, so I had this great base to lean on.

Using slit scan effect was my first idea, so of course I ended up NOT using it, but it drove my graphic research.
I sent a bunch of tests to Stephan Castang. From there we worked on simplifying the sequence, going straight to the point.
That’s when we decided it would be a single shot, a long backward travelling discovering things step by step.

I was in a bit of a midlife crisis and was questionning my envy of making title sequences. I love it, but the chain of command is often very frustrating. So I was taking a step back from this, when producer Cassandre Warnauts called me.

We had worked together in the past and trust each other.
She introduced me to Stephan Castang, and we matched immediately.
It was an artistic crush : we had the same references, talked the same language. I loved the screenplay, its provocative side.
It was one of those rare project were everything goes smoothly and you feel blessed to do what you do.
I’m proud of the result and super happy both the audience and the professionals like it as well.

And I ended up winning both “Art Directors Club award” and the “Rosalie prize”, for best opening sequence in France.

"Impressive opening credits" (into:screens)

"Superbe générique" (les échos)

" Dès le générique très stylisé, on sait que l'on va voir un film singulier et novateur." (Allociné)

"Le générique ne cache pas son amour à l'esprit graphique de Saul Bass" (Médiapart)

"Génial" (Zickma)
